description: A solo developer building an offline-ready health monitoring and emergency guidance app to help astronauts track vitals, detect spaceflight health risks early, and stay safe on deep-space missions.
summary: AegisMed Orbital is a web dashboard that helps keep astronauts healthy on long missions. It watches vital signs, predicts problems before they become critical, and combines them with live NASA and NOAA space weather and the real position of the ISS. It runs on a laptop in mission control and on a phone or tablet in space.
details:
On missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts are far from hospitals, and microgravity, radiation and stress change the body in ways that need constant watching. AegisMed Orbital is a crew health command center that works like this:

  1. Sense: it shows six vital signs for each crew member (heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, core temperature, sleep and stress), each marked Nominal, Warning or Critical. A real Bluetooth heart-rate sensor can replace the simulated heart rate.
  2. Predict: an early-warning system analyses the trend of each vital and estimates when it will leave its safe range, so the crew is warned before it turns red.
  3. Act: an emergency simulator (solar flare, stress spike, fluid shift) shows protocols. The app also has a full-screen body scan, an interactive body map with spaceflight hazards, a spacewalk (EVA) readiness check, a live ECG, daily countermeasures (exercise, hydration, light), a medical supply inventory, a mission log, a flight surgeon chat, and a printable health report.
  4. Connect to space: the app uses real data from NASA and NOAA for the ISS position, solar flares, X-ray and proton radiation levels, geomagnetic activity, live images of the Sun, the aurora forecast, Earth from space, asteroids and natural events.

Crew members can be added, edited and removed, and the app supports voice commands and a mission-control wall mode.

What benefits does it have?

  • It gives crews an early warning instead of a late alarm.
  • It links body signals to the space environment, such as radiation from a solar flare, in one place.
  • It supports crews who can’t wait for help from Earth, with clear protocols and checklists.
  • It works on any device with a browser and needs no special equipment.
  • It keeps the crew’s daily health habits (exercise, hydration, sleep, light) visible and easy to track.

What is the intended impact?
To make long-duration spaceflight safer by helping crews and flight surgeons notice health problems sooner and respond faster. The same idea of trend-based early warnings could also help remote and isolated communities on Earth, such as polar stations, ships and rural clinics.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework.
  • Libraries: Three.js for the 3D Earth and space scene, Leaflet for the interactive map.
  • Browser features: Canvas and SVG for charts and animations, Web Bluetooth for the heart-rate sensor, Web Speech for voice commands.
  • Data sources: NASA DONKI, NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory, NASA EPIC, NASA NeoWs and APOD, NASA EONET, NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, and the Where the ISS at? API.
  • Software: Visual Studio Code for development, Netlify for hosting.
  • Hardware: no special hardware is needed. A Bluetooth heart-rate strap or smartwatch is optional.

How is your project creative?

  • It looks and feels like a real mission control screen, with a 3D Earth, an orbiting ISS, a glowing scan line and a full-screen body scan, instead of a plain spreadsheet of numbers.
  • The space environment changes the app itself. A solar flare sends a shockwave across the screen, turns the Earth red and changes the vitals.
  • It joins two things that are usually separate: crew health data and live space weather.
  • It is built to be used, with voice commands for floating astronauts, a guided tour, and a design that works on both a laptop and a phone.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Honesty about data: the ISS position, flares, space weather and images are real. The crew vitals, crew records, supplies and accumulated radiation dose are simulated. The app says so on its Data sources page, and its thresholds are for demonstration, not medical advice.
  • Different users: one app for mission control on a laptop and for astronauts on a tablet or phone.
  • Safety and clarity: every status is written in words as well as color, and alerts come with clear next steps.
  • Reliability: feeds that fail show a clear message and the rest of the app keeps working.
  • Performance: a 3D quality setting and fewer visual effects on phones.
  • Next steps: wearables for the whole crew, models that run on board, and safe ranges checked with flight surgeons.
